promptText: In the 'sandwich' mental model, what is the structural difference between an input guardrail and an output guardrail?
options: Input guardrails protect the model/business from what the user or upstream content is trying to do; output guardrails protect the user/business from what the model actually produced
Input guardrails are optional hardening while output guardrails are the only mandatory layer
Input guardrails always use LLM-as-judge while output guardrails only use regex
Input guardrails run after the model responds and output guardrails run before the prompt is assembled
explanation: The two check for structurally different problems: input guardrails guard against jailbreaks, injected instructions, and forbidden requests before the model sees them, while output guardrails catch hallucinations, leaked prompts, and policy-violating content the model itself generated.

promptText: Which of the four guardrail technique families eliminates an entire class of violations 'by construction' rather than detecting a violation after it occurs?
options: Deterministic rules (regex/denylists)
Purpose-trained classifiers
LLM-as-judge
Structural/schema constraints
explanation: Forcing output into a constrained shape (a JSON schema, an enum, an allow-listed action set) makes an entire category of malformed or off-policy output structurally impossible, the same way a compiler makes a type mismatch impossible, rather than detecting it after generation.

promptText: In the guardrail precision/recall confusion matrix, what does a false negative represent?
options: A benign message that was wrongly blocked
A genuine policy violation that the guardrail incorrectly let through
A violation that was correctly blocked
A benign message that was correctly allowed
explanation: A false negative is a missed violation — content that actually violates policy but the guardrail allowed through — which is why it is called the dangerous failure mode for high-severity categories like self-harm.

promptText: Why should a self-harm classifier threshold be set differently than a mild-profanity classifier threshold in an internal developer tool?
options: Self-harm classifiers are technically incapable of producing false positives
The acceptable cost of a false negative differs enormously between the two categories, so each needs its own precision/recall trade-off
Profanity filters cannot use classifiers at all, only regex
Both should always share one global threshold to keep the pipeline simple
explanation: For self-harm, a missed violation is severe and often irreversible, so the threshold is tuned toward recall even at the cost of more false positives; for profanity in a developer tool, false positives cause real productivity harm, so the threshold is tuned toward precision instead.

promptText: What is the primary weakness of a hand-maintained denylist used as a standalone guardrail?
options: It is too slow to run in a request's critical path
It requires a GPU to evaluate
It is trivially evaded through paraphrase, novel phrasing, or obfuscation the list was never written to catch
It cannot be combined with any other guardrail layer
explanation: A denylist only knows the exact patterns it was given; users and attackers adapt within days by rephrasing or encoding around it, which is why it must be layered with statistical or model-based detection rather than used alone.

promptText: A user politely asks a banking assistant to 'write a poem about our competitor's new product.' Which guardrail category is specifically designed to catch this, when a toxicity classifier would not?
options: PII detection guardrail
Toxicity/safety classifier
Topical (scope) guardrail
Structural output validator
explanation: A topical guardrail constrains the conversation to the intended domain even when a request is polite and non-toxic; toxicity classifiers have no concept of 'off-brief but harmless,' so this kind of drift sails straight through them.

promptText: Why should documents retrieved by a RAG pipeline pass through the same input guardrail scanning as raw user messages, even though the vector store is owned by the application team?
options: Vector databases silently corrupt text encoding, which the scan repairs

Retrieved content re-enters the prompt through the same channel the model reads instructions from, and if the corpus contains any user-generated or externally sourced content, it can carry an injection payload
Guardrail scanning is required by the embedding model's license terms
It reduces the number of tokens sent to the model, lowering cost
explanation: The model has no reliable way to distinguish 'trusted content from our vector store' from instruction-like phrasing; 'we own the data source' is not the same as 'the data source cannot contain adversarial text,' especially if any of it originated upstream from user-generated content.

promptText: A hosted moderation classifier that guards against self-harm content starts timing out intermittently. What is generally the correct default failure policy for this specific category, and why?
options: Fail-open always, because availability must never be sacrificed for a content check
Fail-closed, because a missed self-harm violation is a severe, potentially irreversible harm that outweighs the availability cost
Fail-open, because the deterministic regex layer alone is always sufficient for self-harm detection
The failure policy is a purely technical default set by the circuit breaker library, not a product decision
explanation: Fail-open vs. fail-closed is a policy decision driven by the severity of what that guardrail protects against; a high-severity, low-frequency harm like self-harm content usually warrants fail-closed even at the cost of availability, unlike a lower-severity category such as mild profanity.

promptText: In a Spring AI advisor chain, why must an input guardrail advisor's getOrder() give it higher precedence than the RetrievalAugmentationAdvisor?
options: Otherwise the guardrail only ever scans the user's raw message and never sees retrieved documents injected afterward, leaving that channel completely unguarded
Advisor order only affects logging output, not which content gets scanned
Retrieval must always run first to reduce the token count the guardrail has to process
Spring AI requires guardrail advisors to run last by framework convention
explanation: If the input guardrail runs after retrieval augmentation injects external content into the prompt, it silently misses everything the RAG pipeline pulled in — exactly the injection surface the next chapter focuses on.

promptText: When should a PII guardrail redact detected data rather than block the request outright?
options: Always redact and never block, regardless of context
When the PII is incidental to the user's actual intent and the interaction remains useful once it is stripped out, unlike when the request is fundamentally about revealing another person's data
Only when the PII appears inside a JSON-structured tool call argument
Block whenever any PII-shaped string appears anywhere in the input
explanation: Redaction is appropriate when PII is incidental (a phone number embedded in an otherwise answerable support message); blocking is appropriate when the request's actual purpose cannot be safely fulfilled at all, since redacting there just hides evidence of the underlying violation.

promptText: What is the key trade-off between an NLI entailment model and an LLM-as-judge call for a groundedness guardrail?
options: NLI is fast, cheap, and purpose-built but struggles with claims requiring multi-hop reasoning across several chunks; LLM-as-judge handles nuance across chunks at meaningfully higher latency and cost
NLI models require no training data while LLM-as-judge models require labeled data
LLM-as-judge is always cheaper because it reuses the production model's cache
NLI can only be applied to structured JSON outputs, never free text
explanation: NLI models classify entailment quickly and deterministically but are weaker on multi-hop or nuanced numerical/temporal claims; LLM-as-judge reasons more flexibly but inherits real latency, cost, and its own fallibility, which is why production systems often run NLI first and escalate ambiguous cases to the judge.

promptText: When guardrailing a streamed response with a rolling-window buffering strategy, why is the window sized to a sentence or clause boundary rather than a fixed token count?
options: Fixed-token windows are technically impossible to implement in a streaming API
Guardrail checks (classifiers, rules) work more reliably against complete semantic units, so cutting mid-clause increases both false positives and false negatives
Sentence-sized windows always eliminate the time-to-first-token latency benefit entirely
Token counts are unavailable until the entire response has finished generating
explanation: Scoring a fragment cut off mid-sentence gives a classifier or rule less coherent text to evaluate, degrading accuracy; aligning the window to a semantic boundary keeps checks accurate while still releasing content faster than buffering the entire response.

promptText: A jailbreak gets a model to reason step by step toward unsafe content across several sentences, then states the payload in fluent, unremarkable-sounding final phrasing. An output guardrail scans only the final response text for known bad patterns and classifier-scored categories. Why can this jailbreak still succeed despite the output guardrail?
options: Output guardrails cannot technically be applied to generated text, only to structured JSON

The output guardrail only sees the final surface phrasing; if that phrasing is novel enough to avoid known patterns and the classifier's trained categories, nothing in the pipeline evaluated the reasoning process that led there
Output guardrails always run before the model call, so they never see the response at all
Input guardrails would have caught this same payload with 100% certainty, making the output layer redundant
explanation: Guardrails inspect content, not the model's internal reasoning; a deterministic or classifier layer scoring only the final text can miss a novel, fluently-phrased payload, which is exactly why layered detection and defense-in-depth (not any single filter) are the actual mitigation.

promptText: A staff engineer decides an internal engineering assistant's topical guardrail should be tuned toward precision, while the organization's self-harm classifier is tuned toward recall. What single principle explains why these two categories warrant opposite tuning postures?
options: The acceptable cost of a false negative differs by category: missing a self-harm case is severe and often irreversible, so recall is prioritized, whereas a topical false positive erodes adoption and trust more than an occasional off-topic answer costs, so precision is prioritized
Topical guardrails cannot generate false positives by definition, so precision is the only measurable axis
Self-harm classifiers are exempt from precision/recall trade-offs because they always operate at 100% accuracy
Internal tools never need any guardrail tuning since there is no external user to protect
explanation: Threshold posture is a policy decision driven by the real-world cost of each error type: a category where a miss is catastrophic gets tuned for recall, while a category where over-blocking damages trust and adoption gets tuned for precision — the same underlying framework applied to different severity profiles.

promptText: Why does defense-in-depth against guardrail evasion require layers that fail for structurally different reasons, rather than simply stacking more checks of the same type?
options: Adding more regex rules of the same kind scales linearly and is equivalent to adding a different detection mechanism

An evasion technique effective against one layer type often does not transfer to a structurally different layer — homoglyph substitution defeats exact-match denylists but not a semantic classifier, and fluent paraphrase defeats a trained classifier but not an LLM-as-judge reasoning about intent — so an attacker must defeat every distinct mechanism simultaneously
Defense-in-depth exists mainly to reduce latency by parallelizing identical checks
Denylists and classifiers share identical blind spots, so layering them provides no additional protection
explanation: The value of layering isn't just 'more checks' — it's that structurally different mechanisms fail independently for different reasons, turning a single clever bypass technique into a much harder problem, since it now has to beat every layer's distinct failure mode at once.
